chunks: And Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Musa ibn Bakr from Muhammad ibn Ali from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

When a slave marries a free woman, the master has the right to separate them, and if the master marries the slave to a free woman, he has the right to separate them. These two rulings do not contradict what we have previously established, because in the first report it is stated that he has the right to take her back without divorce whenever he wishes, and in the second report it is stated that he has the right to separate them; neither explicitly states that this right exists while she is in his ownership or the slave is in his ownership. If this is not explicit in its apparent meaning, we interpret it as him having this right by selling her or selling him, so that their sale constitutes separation between them, as we will explain in a separate chapter, and that which indicates this is here.
ai.seo_question: What are the legal mechanisms for a master to separate a slave from his free wife in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar clarifies the juristic mechanism of 'firqah' (separation) in the marriage of a slave to a free woman, asserting that the master's right to dissolve the union is not limited to formal divorce but extends to selling the slave or the wife. Shaykh al-Tusi employs this text to reconcile apparent contradictions in earlier hadiths by interpreting the master's authority as inherent to ownership, thereby allowing separation through alienation of property rather than solely through marital decree.
